slides.title: Every rule is one sentence.
slides.text: A {rule} says: this role may do these things, on this data, until then. Nothing more. Everything anyone may ever do with your data is written in rules like this one.

slides.title: What a rule can allow.
slides.text: Each entry in “do” is one thing a role may do. Some are about the content, some about carrying it, and two are about rules themselves.
list: Rules: admin (write any rule), share (pass on a narrower one).
Engine dos, like find or search, need no entry of their own: read is enough.

slides.title: Conditions make a rule narrower.
slides.text: Each “do” can carry {conditions}: only this part of the data, only entries that match, only with two signatures, only so many times.

slides.title: Every rule expires.
slides.text: No rule lasts forever by accident. Each one has an {expiry}, 30 days unless you choose otherwise. A forgotten share closes by itself.

slides.title: Unchanged rules renew themselves.
slides.text: You don't want your family locked out every month. So a device of an admin quietly renews every rule that hasn't changed, a week before it ends. Rules you changed or removed simply run out.

slides.title: Only the owner never expires.
slides.text: The rule the seal signed at birth names the owner. It has no expiry, so data can never end up with nobody allowed to look after it. Only the owner can hand it over to another identity. Every other rule expires.

slides.title: Under the hood, a rule is a capability.
slides.text: Each rule is a signed token, a {capability}, like a Biscuit. It carries its own proof: who signed it, and why they were allowed to, all the way back to the seal. Any device can check it offline. Nobody can forge it.

slides.title: Passing a rule on only narrows it.
slides.text: If home's rule allows share, Mia can give a role of her own, “grandma's”, a rule of its own: she adds a block to the token. A block can only take things away, shorten the expiry or add conditions. It can never add.

slides.title: Every device checks the same four things.
slides.text: Before a change goes in, or before a single byte goes out, a device checks the rule behind it.
list: Every signature in the proof is valid, back to the seal.
What's being done is listed in its “do”.

slides.title: Ending a rule early.
slides.text: You don't have to wait for the expiry. An admin writes a {revoke}: a signed event in the history that says “this rule is over”. It travels like any other change.

slides.title: When time runs out, anyone may say so.
slides.text: Devices are often offline, and a device can lie about its time, so no clock decides. Once a rule's date has passed for it, any peer that can read the rules writes a {lapse}: the same kind of event as a revoke. It can only end a rule, never grant anything. From then on, the history decides.

slides.title: Revoke or lapse: one ending, same effect.
slides.text: Whoever wrote it, an {ending} does the same three things on every device. Changes that never saw it are dropped, because the ending wins. The data key turns. And every honest device wipes the keys and copies the rule gave it. Validity follows from the history alone, so every copy agrees.

slides.title: When an admin leaves, the role moves.
slides.text: A removed admin could still write a revoke and pretend it happened before their removal. So when an admin is removed, the role doesn't just get a new key: it is replaced by a {successor role} with a new ID, and everyone else is added again. The ex-admin's old revokes point at a role that no longer counts.

slides.title: Rules, in short.
list: A rule: this role may do these things, on this data, until then.
Data has one owner, an identity; its rule never expires.
Conditions narrow a rule; nothing can widen it.
A revoke or a lapse is an ending: it wins, turns the key and wipes copies.
A removed admin means a successor role.
Under the hood: a signed token any device checks offline.
